title: Aristotle's Logic
orientation: This chapter examines Aristotle's logical writings -- above all the theory of the syllogism, but also the Categories and the Posterior Analytics -- which Russell treats as Aristotle's single most influential contribution, dominant for over two thousand years and still, in his own day, upheld by Catholic philosophy despite being 'as definitely antiquated as Ptolemaic astronomy.' The chapter matters because it shows Russell, himself a founder of modern mathematical logic, delivering a sustained technical critique of the system that blocked logical progress for two millennia, and because it traces the deep metaphysical errors (about 'substance' and 'essence') that Russell believes flowed from Aristotle's underestimated formal mistakes.
historical_background: Russell notes that Aristotle's authority in logic long outlasted his authority in metaphysics: Plato remained supreme in metaphysics through late antiquity, and it was not until the thirteenth century that Christian philosophers granted Aristotle supremacy there too, yet his supremacy in logic 'survived' even the decline of his metaphysical authority after the Renaissance. Russell states this makes it uniquely difficult to treat Aristotle 'historically': unlike his predecessors, whom one can praise without endorsing, Aristotle's logic remains, in Russell's own time, 'a battle-ground.'
philosophical_problems: What makes a deductive inference (a syllogism) valid, and are all valid deductions syllogistic?
Does a universal categorical statement like 'all Greeks are men' presuppose that Greeks actually exist?
How much of our knowledge of general truths is really obtained by deduction, as opposed to induction?
What are 'categories,' and is the notion philosophically useful?
What is the 'essence' of a thing, and is it a fact about the world or merely a fact about how we use words?
Is 'substance' -- a persisting thing underlying its properties -- a genuine metaphysical category or a linguistic illusion?

philosophers_discussed.name: Aristotle
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Primary subject: Russell reconstructs the theory of the syllogism, the doctrine of the Categories, and the treatment of essence and substance in the Posterior Analytics, before subjecting each to detailed logical and metaphysical criticism.

philosophers_discussed.name: Porphyry
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The Neoplatonist commentator on Aristotle's Categories, whose commentary had, per Russell, 'a very notable influence on medieval philosophy,' and who, Russell says, showed 'less caution' than Aristotle himself in treating a species as a kind of substance.

philosophers_discussed.name: Kant
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited as an example of a later philosopher misled by Aristotle's over-estimation of the syllogism: having correctly noticed that mathematics is not syllogistic, Kant wrongly inferred it must rest on special extra-logical principles of equal certainty to logic itself.

core_concepts.name: The syllogism
core_concepts.plain_explanation: A syllogism is a three-step argument with a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion -- the classic example being 'All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal' -- and Aristotle's logic classifies and names many valid patterns of this kind.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aristotle's central logical form, an argument of exactly three parts (major premiss, minor premiss, conclusion) sorted by the scholastics into named figures and moods (e.g. 'Barbara,' 'Celarent,' 'Darii,' 'Ferio' in the first figure), with a second and third figure reducible to the first, and a fourth figure later added by medieval logicians.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It was, for over two thousand years, treated as the complete and exhaustive form of valid deductive reasoning, making it the foundation of formal logic as taught from antiquity through the Middle Ages.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Set out primarily in Aristotle's Prior Analytics.
examples: Barbara: 'All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal.'
Celarent: 'No fishes are rational; all sharks are fishes; therefore no sharks are rational.'
objections: Russell: Aristotle 'does not distinguish' between 'Socrates is a man' (a statement about a named individual) and 'all Greeks are men' (a universal statement of quite different logical form), which is itself 'a mistake' with serious downstream consequences.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Remained the accepted foundation of formal logic until the rise of modern mathematical logic, which Russell himself helped develop.

core_concepts.name: Formal defects: existential import and the particular/universal confusion
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Aristotle treats 'Socrates is a man' and 'all Greeks are men' as the same basic kind of statement, but they are not: 'all Greeks are men' really packs together two separate claims -- 'there are Greeks' and 'if anything is a Greek, it is a man' -- and Aristotle's failure to separate these leads him, and much of later philosophy, into serious confusion about what a general term like 'man' actually refers to.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's critique that Aristotelian universal statements ('all S is P') are ambiguous between a purely hypothetical reading (which does not imply that any S exists) and a reading that presupposes S is non-empty, and that several of Aristotle's syllogisms are valid only under the latter, existentially-loaded reading -- a distinction Aristotle's system never makes explicit.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell traces significant later metaphysical errors to this single formal oversight: treating 'all Greeks' as though it were a kind of subject analogous to 'Socrates' led Aristotle (and, with less caution, Porphyry) to say that a species is, in some sense, a substance, and to conflate predicates of predicates with predicates of the original subject.
core_concepts.historical_origin: A gap in Aristotle's Prior Analytics that Russell diagnoses using the tools of modern logic.
examples: 'All Greeks are men, all Greeks are white, therefore some men are white' is valid only if Greeks actually exist.

Russell's counterexample: 'All golden mountains are mountains, all golden mountains are golden, therefore some mountains are golden' -- valid in form but with a false conclusion, since no golden mountains exist.
competing_positions: The correct, explicit logical treatment (implicit in Russell's own later work) that splits 'all Greeks are men' into an existence claim and a purely hypothetical universal conditional.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Led to what Russell calls a 'source of errors in metaphysics and theory of knowledge' running through much of the philosophical tradition dependent on Aristotelian logic.

core_concepts.name: Metaphysical errors flowing from Aristotle's logical confusions
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Because Aristotle treats 'all men' as though it names a single subject, the way 'Socrates' names one, he ends up thinking a whole species like 'man' can itself be a kind of substance, and this same confusion between particulars and universals later produces the mistaken idea that a class with exactly one member is identical to that member.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's diagnosis that Aristotle's failure to distinguish particulars from universals produced (a) the claim, in the Categories, that a species or genus can be called a 'substance' in a 'secondary' sense, and (b) the invalid inference-pattern that a predicate of a predicate (e.g., 'human' predicated of 'Greek,' which is predicated of 'Socrates') can simply be transferred to the original subject, blurring the particular/universal distinction with, Russell says, 'disastrous consequences to philosophy.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This is Russell's central thesis for why Aristotelian logic is not merely technically flawed but philosophically damaging: formal imprecision about subjects and predicates directly generated centuries of confused metaphysics about universals, unity, and number.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Traced by Russell to Aristotle's own Categories, worsened by Porphyry's less cautious commentary.
examples: 'If I say "Socrates is Greek, all Greeks are human," Aristotle thinks that "human" is a predicate of "Greek"... and obviously "human" is a predicate of "Socrates"' -- but, Russell argues, 'human' is not really a predicate of 'Greek' at all in the same sense.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell says this 'made it impossible to have a correct theory of the number one, and led to endless bad metaphysics about unity' (via the confusion of a one-member class with its sole member).

core_concepts.name: Over-estimation of deduction relative to induction
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Greek philosophers in general, and to a lesser extent Aristotle himself, treated logical deduction as the main road to knowledge, but Russell argues most of what we actually know -- including 'Mr. Smith is mortal' -- really rests on induction (generalizing from many observed cases) rather than on deducing it from a supposedly certain universal premise like 'all men are mortal.'
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's claim that, apart from logic and pure mathematics, virtually all substantive inference outside law and theology (which derive their first principles from an unquestionable text) is inductive rather than deductive, contrary to the excessive prominence Greek philosophy, including Aristotle's own theory of knowledge, gives to deduction from general premises.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It corrects a foundational error about the nature of empirical knowledge: 'all men are mortal' is not itself known with certainty (no living man has yet falsified it), so any inference from it to a particular case is, at bottom, inductive and only probable, not the certain deduction Aristotelian theory of knowledge suggests.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Russell credits Aristotle with being 'less at fault than Plato' here, since Aristotle 'repeatedly admitted the importance of induction' and asked how first premises are known -- but still judges him guilty of 'undue prominence' to deduction overall.
examples: What we really know is closer to 'all men born more than one hundred and fifty years ago are mortal, and so are almost all men born more than one hundred years ago' -- an inductive generalization from observed cases, not a certain universal premise.
competing_positions: Law and theology, which Russell notes are genuine exceptions, since they derive first principles deductively from an 'unquestionable text' (statute books or scripture) rather than from induction over experience.

core_concepts.name: Essence
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Philosophers after Aristotle spoke of a thing's 'essence' -- the properties it cannot lose without ceasing to be itself -- but Russell argues this is really just a fact about how we choose to use a name, not a fact about the world: whether 'being a man' is essential to Socrates depends only on whether we would still call him 'Socrates' if that changed.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aristotle's notion, central to the Posterior Analytics's account of definition and first premisses, that a thing's essential properties are those it cannot change without losing its identity, as opposed to accidental properties (like being happy or sad) that it can change while remaining the same thing; Russell calls this 'a hopelessly muddle-headed notion' whose real content is purely linguistic.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Essence became, per Russell, 'an intimate part of every philosophy subsequent to Aristotle... until we come to modern times,' making its critique essential to understanding a huge stretch of the later philosophical tradition, even though Russell judges the underlying concept confused.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed in Aristotle's Posterior Analytics as the basis for definitions and, ultimately, for the unproved first premisses all demonstration must start from.
examples: Socrates may be sometimes happy, sometimes sad -- accidental properties -- but it is supposed to be of his essence that he is a man, 'though a Pythagorean, who believes in transmigration, will not admit this.'
objections: Russell: 'the question of "essence" is one as to the use of words'; 'the "essence" of Socrates thus consists of those properties in the absence of which we should not use the name "Socrates."' A word may have an essence, but a thing cannot.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Persisted as a core philosophical concept for roughly two thousand years, per Russell, until displaced in modern philosophy.

core_concepts.name: Substance
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Aristotle (and much later philosophy) treats things like 'Socrates' or 'France' as persisting 'substances' underlying their changing properties -- something solid the properties belong to -- but Russell argues this is just a convenient way of bundling many separate events under one name, not a discovery of some further, more 'real' thing beneath them.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The Aristotelian notion (Categories) of substance in its primary sense as an individual thing that is neither predicable of, nor present in, any other subject, later extended (in a 'secondary' sense Russell finds indefensible) to species and genera; Russell argues on independent grounds that substance, taken seriously as something distinct from all its properties, is 'a metaphysical mistake, due to transference to the world-structure of the structure of sentences composed of a subject and a predicate.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is Russell's culminating critique in the chapter: once essence and substance are both dissolved into facts about language, the entire apparatus of Aristotelian metaphysics built on unchanging 'essences' possessed by underlying 'substances' loses its supposed foundation in reality.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Set out in Aristotle's Categories; the 'secondary' sense (species/genus as substance) especially influenced later scholastic metaphysics via Porphyry's commentary.
examples: 'What is Mr. Smith apart from all these occurrences [that we perceive]? A mere imaginary hook, from which the occurrences are supposed to hang.'
Comparison to 'France': just as there is no single thing called 'France' over and above its various parts, so 'Mr. Smith' is only a collective name for a number of occurrences.
objections: Russell's regress argument: if substance is 'the subject of properties, distinct from all its properties,' then removing the properties to imagine the bare substance leaves nothing at all; and two substances cannot even be distinguished, since difference of properties (the only available criterion) presupposes, rather than explains, their being numerically two.
competing_positions: Russell's own alternative: treating apparent 'substances' as convenient bundles of events/occurrences collected under a common name, with no further underlying entity required.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: The 'secondary' sense of substance, per Russell, 'opened the door, in later writers, to much bad metaphysics.'

arguments.title: The Barbara syllogism as the paradigm of valid deduction
arguments.explanation: Russell presents this, and Aristotle's other named syllogistic figures (Celarent, Darii, Ferio), as the historical foundation of formal logic, praiseworthy as 'the beginning of formal logic' even though, Russell insists, they are inadequate 'considered as the end.'
objections: Russell's formal-defects critique: Aristotle does not distinguish 'Socrates is a man' from 'all Greeks are men,' which are logically different in kind (the second has existential import the first does not need).
implications: This conflation, though seemingly minor, is the seed of the deeper metaphysical confusions about substance, essence, and unity that Russell traces through the rest of the chapter.

arguments.title: Russell's critique of existential import in universal statements
premises: 'All Greeks are men, all Greeks are white, therefore some men are white' is treated by Aristotle as simply valid.
But 'all golden mountains are mountains, all golden mountains are golden, therefore some mountains are golden' has exactly the same form.
arguments.conclusion: The first syllogism is valid only because Greeks actually exist; the general Aristotelian form is valid only under a hidden existential assumption that Aristotle's system never makes explicit.
arguments.explanation: Russell constructs the golden-mountains counterexample to show that universal statements like 'all S is P' must be split into an existence claim ('there are S's') and a purely hypothetical claim ('if anything is S, it is P') if the underlying logic of such inferences is to be made precise.
implications: Demonstrates a genuine, technically identifiable flaw at the heart of the traditional syllogistic system, motivating the more rigorous quantificational logic Russell himself helped develop.

arguments.title: The inductive character of general empirical belief ('Mr. Smith is mortal')
premises: We commonly say we know 'Mr. Smith is mortal' because we know 'all men are mortal.'
But 'all men are mortal' is not itself known with certainty; no living man has falsified it, but it 'cannot be certain so long as living men exist.'
What we actually have evidence for is closer to a restricted, probabilistic generalization from observed cases of death at various ages.
arguments.conclusion: Our confidence that Mr. Smith will die rests on induction from observed cases, not on certain deduction from a fully general, certainly known premise.
arguments.explanation: Russell uses this everyday example to argue that Greek philosophy's general over-valuation of deduction, which Aristotle shares to a lesser degree than Plato, misdescribes how most substantive knowledge is actually obtained.
implications: Establishes Russell's broader claim that 'all the important inferences outside logic and pure mathematics are inductive, not deductive,' with law and theology as the sole exceptions (deriving first principles from an unquestionable text).

arguments.title: The regress argument against substance
premises: A substance is supposed to be the subject of properties, distinct from all of them.
If we mentally remove all of a substance's properties to consider the 'bare' substance itself, nothing remains to be considered.
Two substances can only be distinguished by a difference of properties, but difference of properties itself presupposes that the substances are already numerically two.
arguments.conclusion: 'Substance,' taken as something genuinely distinct from and underlying its properties, is 'a metaphysical mistake, due to transference to the world-structure of the structure of sentences composed of a subject and a predicate' -- merely 'a convenient way of collecting events into bundles.'
arguments.explanation: Russell develops this argument himself, using the Categories's definition of substance as his starting point, to show that Aristotle's primary metaphysical category cannot survive close logical scrutiny once we ask what, exactly, a 'bare' substance stripped of properties could be.
implications: Undercuts the entire substance/essence apparatus at the foundation of Aristotelian and much subsequent metaphysics, supporting Russell's overall verdict that these doctrines are 'wholly false.'

key_distinctions: 'Socrates is a man' (statement about a named individual) vs. 'all Greeks are men' (a general statement with hidden existential structure)
The existence claim ('there are Greeks') vs. the purely hypothetical claim ('if anything is a Greek, it is a man') packed into a single Aristotelian universal statement
Deduction (certain but not knowledge-generating) vs. induction (probable but knowledge-generating) as sources of substantive belief
'Substance' in Aristotle's primary sense (an individual thing) vs. his 'secondary' sense (a species or genus), which Russell calls 'indefensible'
Essential properties (which a thing cannot lose without losing its name/identity) vs. accidental properties (which it can lose while remaining 'the same')
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Russell notes that Aristotle's logical innovations represented 'a very admirable' advance on all his predecessors, including Plato, and that Aristotle was 'less at fault than Plato' in over-valuing deduction, since he alone among the major Greek philosophers 'repeatedly admitted the importance of induction.' The chapter's critique of 'essence' and 'substance' is framed as the origin point of a confusion that then runs through 'every philosophy subsequent to Aristotle... until we come to modern times.'
connections_to_later_philosophers: Russell traces the Categories's influence through Porphyry's Neoplatonic commentary into medieval scholastic philosophy, and shows how Kant, correctly noticing that mathematics is not syllogistic, was nonetheless misled by residual respect for Aristotle into positing special extra-logical principles for mathematics rather than questioning the primacy of the syllogism itself. Russell closes by asserting that 'practically every advance in science, in logic, or in philosophy' in the modern era 'has had to be made in the teeth of the opposition from Aristotle's disciples' -- implicitly including his own and Whitehead's work in mathematical logic among these advances.
religion_science_culture_context: Russell notes that, in his own day, 'all Catholic teachers of philosophy and many others still obstinately reject the discoveries of modern logic, and adhere with a strange tenacity to a system which is as definitely antiquated as Ptolemaic astronomy' -- a direct comparison between Aristotelian logic's persistence in religious education and the earlier persistence of Ptolemaic astronomy against Copernican reform.
russell_presentation: Russell first presents Aristotle's theory of the syllogism largely on its own terms -- the major/minor premise/conclusion structure, the named figures (Barbara, Celarent, Darii, Ferio), and the reduction of later figures to the first -- crediting it as historically important, 'the beginning of formal logic.' He then organizes his critique under three explicit headings Aristotle's system invites: (1) formal defects internal to the system, focused on the unexamined existential import of universal statements and its metaphysical fallout (the species-as-substance error, the predicate-of-predicate error, the one-member-class error); (2) the over-estimation of the syllogism relative to other valid deductive forms, illustrated with ordinary arithmetic and Kant's resulting confusion about mathematical reasoning; and (3) the over-estimation of deduction generally relative to induction, illustrated with the 'Mr. Smith is mortal' example. Russell then turns to two further Aristotelian texts, the Categories (ten categories; the primary/secondary senses of substance) and the Posterior Analytics (the theory of essence as the basis of definition and first premisses), tracing both concepts -- essence and substance -- back to what he argues are purely linguistic facts mistaken for metaphysical discoveries.
critical_context: Russell's verdict, stated explicitly rather than left implicit, closes the chapter: 'the Aristotelian doctrines with which we have been concerned in this chapter are wholly false, with the exception of the formal theory of the syllogism, which is unimportant,' and 'any person in the present day who wishes to learn logic will be wasting his time if he reads Aristotle or any of his disciples.' Russell is careful to add a historically sympathetic qualification alongside this harsh technical judgment: Aristotle's logical writings 'show great ability, and would have been useful to mankind if they had appeared at a time when intellectual originality was still active,' but their misfortune was to arrive at the end of the creative period of Greek thought and then be treated as unquestionable authority for two thousand years.
key_takeaways: Aristotle's syllogism (major premise, minor premise, conclusion, exemplified by Barbara) was treated as the complete theory of valid deduction for over two thousand years.

Russell identifies a genuine formal defect: Aristotle conflates 'Socrates is a man' with 'all Greeks are men,' ignoring that universal statements carry a hidden, unexamined existential assumption -- shown by the 'golden mountains' counterexample.

This formal conflation produced deep metaphysical errors: treating a species as a kind of substance, treating a predicate of a predicate as a predicate of the original subject, and confusing a one-member class with its member.

Aristotle over-estimated the syllogism (most deductive reasoning, including mathematics, is not syllogistic) and over-estimated deduction generally (most substantive knowledge, like 'Mr. Smith is mortal,' is really inductive).
Russell argues 'essence' is really just a fact about how we choose to use a name, and 'substance' is merely a convenient way of bundling events under a common name, not a genuine underlying entity.

Russell's final verdict: Aristotelian logic and metaphysics (apart from the unimportant formal syllogism) are 'wholly false,' though historically Aristotle's genuine ability was wasted by arriving at the end, not the start, of Greek intellectual creativity.
study_notes:
This chapter rewards close, patient reading because Russell is doing genuine technical philosophy, not just historical summary -- and he tells you his plan explicitly: three numbered criticisms (formal defects, over-estimation of the syllogism, over-estimation of deduction). Use that numbering as your own outline while reading; each of Russell's examples (golden mountains, the arithmetic change-counting example, 'Mr. Smith is mortal') is a deliberately chosen illustration of exactly one of the three criticisms, so identifying which criticism an example supports is a good comprehension check.

The single most important idea to master is the existential-import problem: 'all Greeks are men' secretly contains two separate claims ('there are Greeks' and 'if Greek, then man'), and Aristotle's logic never separates them. Once you see this, you can trace its consequences forward through the rest of the chapter -- the mistaken idea that a species is a kind of substance, and the mistaken idea that a one-member class is identical with its member, both stem from treating 'all Greeks' grammatically like a proper name such as 'Socrates.'

The chapter's second half, on essence and substance, is best read as Russell performing a kind of linguistic therapy on inherited metaphysical concepts: in both cases, his strategy is to ask 'what, in the actual use of words, does this concept really track?' and to argue that the answer is a fact about naming conventions, not a fact about some further hidden entity in the world. The 'France' analogy for substance, and the transmigration example for essence, are the two illustrations worth remembering, since they show concretely how a plausible-sounding metaphysical claim dissolves once its linguistic basis is exposed.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A three-part logical argument with a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion, like 'All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal.'
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Aristotle's central deductive form, classified by the scholastics into named figures and moods (e.g., Barbara, Celarent, Darii, Ferio in the first figure), long treated as the exhaustive model of valid deductive inference.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The hidden assumption, in a statement like 'all Greeks are men,' that Greeks actually exist.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The implicit claim that the subject class of a universal statement is non-empty, which Russell argues Aristotle's logic never separates from the purely hypothetical content of universal statements, producing formally invalid inferences when the subject class is empty (e.g., 'all golden mountains').
related_concepts: Formal defects: existential import and the particular/universal confusion

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The properties a thing supposedly cannot lose without ceasing to be that thing.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Aristotle's notion, central to the Posterior Analytics, of the properties constitutive of a thing's identity, which Russell argues reduces, on analysis, to a fact about which properties are required for continued application of a given name.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea of a persisting 'thing' that underlies and owns its changing properties, like the 'real' Mr. Smith beneath everything he does and experiences.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Aristotle's category (Categories) of an individual thing not predicable of, nor present in, any subject, taken by Russell to be a metaphysical illusion generated by the subject-predicate structure of ordinary sentences, rather than a genuine feature of reality.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Aristotle's list of the ten most basic kinds of thing a word can signify: substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, state, action, and affection.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The classification, set out in Aristotle's Categories, of the fundamental kinds of predication, which Russell says is offered 'with no suggestion of any principle' governing why these ten and no others were chosen, and which he finds unclear as a philosophical notion.

questions.prompt: What is a syllogism, and what are the three parts Aristotle identifies in one?
questions.answer: A three-part deductive argument consisting of a major premiss, a minor premiss, and a conclusion -- e.g., 'All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal.'
questions.explanation: This structure, named 'Barbara' in this instance, is the paradigmatic form Aristotle's logic builds on.

questions.prompt: Explain, using Russell's golden-mountains example, the formal defect he identifies in Aristotelian universal statements.
questions.answer: 'All golden mountains are mountains, all golden mountains are golden, therefore some mountains are golden' has the same valid-looking form as Aristotle's syllogisms, but its conclusion is false because no golden mountains exist -- showing that such syllogisms are valid only under a hidden assumption that the subject class ('all Greeks,' 'all golden mountains') is non-empty, an assumption Aristotle's system leaves unexamined.
questions.explanation: This is Russell's central technical critique of the syllogism.

questions.prompt: Contrast deduction and induction as sources of knowledge, using Russell's 'Mr. Smith is mortal' example.
questions.answer: We say we know Mr. Smith is mortal by deduction from 'all men are mortal,' but that premise is not itself certainly known (it could not be certain while living men exist); what we actually rely on is an inductive generalization from many observed cases of human mortality at various ages, which yields only probability, not certainty, but does supply genuinely new knowledge.
questions.explanation: Russell uses this to argue Greek philosophy, including Aristotle, over-valued deduction relative to induction.

questions.prompt: What are Aristotle's ten categories, and what is Russell's assessment of the concept of 'category' itself?
questions.answer: Substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, state, action, and affection; Russell says he has 'never been able to understand' what 'category' precisely means and does not believe the term is philosophically useful, noting Aristotle gives no principle explaining why these ten and no others were chosen.
questions.explanation: This is one of the more skeptical passages in the chapter.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Russell's regress argument against 'substance' as something distinct from a thing's properties.
questions.answer: A substance is supposed to be the subject of properties, distinct from all of them; but removing all the properties to consider the bare substance leaves nothing to consider; and two substances could only be distinguished by differing properties, yet difference of properties already presupposes they are numerically two -- so substance cannot coherently be made out as something separate from its properties.
questions.explanation: Russell concludes substance is 'merely a convenient way of collecting events into bundles.'

questions.prompt: According to Russell, what is 'essence' really a fact about, rather than a fact about the world?
questions.answer: It is a fact about the use of words -- the essence of Socrates consists of those properties in the absence of which we should not use the name 'Socrates'; a word may have an essence, but a thing cannot.
questions.explanation: Russell calls the traditional notion of essence 'hopelessly muddle-headed' despite its long historical importance.

questions.prompt: What is Russell's overall verdict on Aristotle's logical and metaphysical doctrines discussed in this chapter?
questions.answer: That they are 'wholly false, with the exception of the formal theory of the syllogism, which is unimportant,' though he credits Aristotle's genuine ability and notes the tragedy of its historical timing, arriving at the end rather than the beginning of Greek intellectual creativity.
questions.explanation: Russell separates the harshness of his technical judgment from a measure of historical sympathy for Aristotle himself.

quiz.prompt: What does Russell's 'golden mountains' example illustrate?
options: That syllogisms with an empty subject class can appear valid but yield false conclusions
That Aristotle rejected the existence of mountains
quiz.explanation: It shows the hidden existential assumption behind Aristotelian universal statements.
quiz.related_concept: Formal defects: existential import and the particular/universal confusion

quiz.prompt: Russell argues that, apart from logic and pure mathematics, virtually all substantive knowledge is obtained by ___, not deduction.
quiz.explanation: Russell argues most knowledge outside logic/mathematics (and law/theology) is inductive.
quiz.related_concept: Over-estimation of deduction relative to induction

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, which two fields are genuine exceptions to the rule that substantive knowledge is inductive?
quiz.explanation: These derive their first principles deductively from an unquestionable text.
quiz.related_concept: Over-estimation of deduction relative to induction

quiz.prompt: Russell argues that 'essence' names a real feature of the world independent of how we use names.
quiz.explanation: Russell argues essence is purely a fact about naming conventions: 'a word may have an essence, but a thing cannot.'

quiz.prompt: What is Russell's regress objection to 'substance' as something distinct from a thing's properties?
options: Substances cannot have any properties at all
Removing all properties leaves nothing to consider as the 'bare' substance, and two substances cannot be distinguished except by properties, which presupposes their being already two
Substance is simply another word for essence
quiz.explanation: This is Russell's own constructed argument against taking substance as a genuine underlying entity.

quiz.prompt: Match each error to its cause: (1) species treated as substance, (2) one-member class treated as identical to its member, (3) Kant's mistaken view of mathematics.
options: (1) and (2) both stem from Aristotle's particular/universal conflation; (3) stems from over-estimating the syllogism as the sole form of deduction
(1) stems from over-estimating deduction; (2) stems from the Categories alone; (3) stems from the theory of essence
All three stem from the same single cause: existential import
None of these are discussed in the chapter
quiz.explanation: Russell traces (1) and (2) to the particular/universal conflation, and (3) to Aristotle's over-valuation of the syllogism specifically.
quiz.related_concept: Metaphysical errors flowing from Aristotle's logical confusions

quiz.prompt: Russell's overall verdict is that Aristotle's logical and metaphysical doctrines discussed in this chapter are entirely false with one unimportant exception.
quiz.explanation: Russell states this explicitly, exempting only the (unimportant) formal theory of the syllogism.

quiz.prompt: Why does Russell say it is historically unfortunate, rather than simply Aristotle's personal failing, that his logic became a two-thousand-year dogma?
options: Because Aristotle intended his logic only as a joke
Because his logical writings arrived at the end of the creative period of Greek thought and were then treated as unquestionable authority, rather than as one stage in continuing progress
Because Aristotle's logic was never actually read until the Renaissance
Because Aristotle himself demanded it be treated as infallible
quiz.explanation: Russell credits Aristotle's genuine ability while blaming the historical accident of timing for the resulting stagnation.

essay_prompts.prompt: Analyze how Russell traces a single formal defect (the unexamined existential import of universal statements) through to specific later metaphysical errors (species-as-substance, the one-member-class confusion). Is this a persuasive account of how a technical logical mistake can produce centuries of metaphysical confusion?
rubric: Accurately explains the existential-import defect with the golden-mountains example
Accurately traces at least two downstream metaphysical errors to this defect
Evaluates whether the causal story is persuasive

essay_prompts.prompt: Evaluate Russell's argument that 'substance' is merely 'a convenient way of collecting events into bundles' rather than a genuine underlying entity. Does his regress argument succeed, and what, if anything, is lost by giving up the traditional notion of substance?
rubric: Considers a serious objection or alternative defense of substance
Discusses the practical/metaphysical stakes of abandoning the concept

essay_prompts.prompt: Compare Russell's treatment of 'essence' with his treatment of 'substance' in this chapter. Are they, at bottom, the same kind of critique applied twice, or are they meaningfully different arguments?
rubric: Accurately states Russell's critique of essence
Accurately states Russell's critique of substance
Identifies structural similarities and/or differences between the two critiques
